key_findings.finding: The documented near-term bottlenecks include distribution, controls and aging storage.

key_findings.page_references: state-01 PDF pages 1â€“2; state-05 PDF page 1
key_findings.implication: Do not frame local operators as unaware of infrastructure problems or assume drilling is their principal immediate need.

key_findings.finding: Published dates are a schedule, not proof that construction has occurred.
key_findings.evidence_status: Planned milestones in December 2025 memo; June 2026 environmental action located
key_findings.details: Memo schedules financing closing March 31, 2026; feasibility-report completion August 31, 2026; design January 31, 2027; construction August 1, 2027â€“January 31, 2028. This archive does not establish actual closing, feasibility-report delivery, current schedule or contractor award.

key_findings.finding: The June 2026 environmental approval has a narrower footprint than every alternative contemplated.
key_findings.details: The finding covers two replacement sections along Highways 118 and 170, SCADA and two ground tanks. It excludes the Ron Read Road Alternate, Segment 3, from this finding. No loop extensions are included. It identifies trenchless crossings at Long Draw and Rough Run and requires relevant floodplain approval. Maps are included in the archived original.
key_findings.implication: The current project repairs existing service; it is not approval for region-wide new connections.

key_findings.finding: The regional plan recommends a larger water-loss strategy, but that is not an $8.52 million construction award.
key_findings.evidence_status: Adopted planning strategy E-6, October 2025 plan
key_findings.details: Appendix 5A assumes eight miles of six-inch replacement main, $8,520,000 capital and potential savings of 12 acre-feet/year. Its water-loss premise is the 2020 audit: 45 acre-feet of real losses, 27%. That historical measure is not a current loss rate, and apparent/non-revenue losses are different measures.
key_findings.page_references: Printed 5A-5 / PDF page 283; cost basis September 2023 in cost appendix
key_findings.implication: A larger conservation need has already been recognized, but existing funded work and future recommended work need to be reconciled.

key_findings.finding: The regional plan explicitly identifies the aquifer study that this project had independently proposed.
key_findings.evidence_status: Adopted research recommendation, not proof that the study is funded or complete
key_findings.details: Southern Brewster Cretaceous limestone supplies require characterization of geographic extent, sustainable yield and water quality. The plan describes two Study Butte wells and uncertainty about pumping interactions with wells roughly ten miles away.
key_findings.page_references: Printed 8-6 / PDF page 586; printed 3-38 / PDF page 174
key_findings.implication: A useful entrepreneurial role could be assembling a utility-led, project-specific assessment around an already acknowledged regional research gap.
key_findings.update_2026_10_23: A February 2026 Steve Finch conceptual-model presentation has now been found on the Brewster County GCD website and reviewed. It substantially advances the framework/recharge/quality work, but does not quantify sustainable yield. See santa-elena-findings.json.

key_findings.finding: Planning supply is not available spare capacity.
key_findings.evidence_status: Adopted model quantities, not recent meter or pump-test measurements
key_findings.details: For 2030 the plan assigns Study Butte 387 acre-feet/year existing supply and 341 demand; Lajitas 331 supply and 244 demand. Neither is projected to have a planning deficit. The figures do not establish treatment headroom, daily peak capacity, water for transfer, or service availability for unconnected households. County-Other is separate from named WUGs and extends beyond the proposed local service area.
key_findings.page_references: Table 2-2 / PDF111; Table 3-3 / PDF141; state-22 PDF2
key_findings.implication: Define the local footprint and uncovered population before estimating regional demand; do not add all Brewster County supplies as water available for Terlingua.

key_findings.finding: A state program can support planning without the entrepreneur paying for a duplicate study.
key_findings.evidence_status: Current WUTAP published terms; no Study Butte participation located
key_findings.details: WUTAP offers selected systems up to $150,000 in services, no financial match; system staff must participate. Applications are accepted at any time and selected by need and available funds. Services include project needs/viability, rates, operating/financial procedures and funding applications. TWDB contracts with the provider; it is not $150,000 cash given to the entrepreneur.
key_findings.implication: A willing utility is the practical sponsor; investigate whether it already receives overlapping assistance.

key_findings.finding: TWSCG has a relevant near-term application window, but eligibility and duplication restrictions matter.
key_findings.evidence_status: Current funding opportunity, not an award
key_findings.details: The current page gives a January 13, 2027, 11:59 p.m. CST deadline, $50 million statewide and 100% grants. The linked September 10, 2026 plan caps a project at $5 million and one application per entity. Nonprofit Chapter 67 WSCs serving existing residential customers are eligible; primarily commercial/industrial and private utilities are excluded. Previously funded TWDB activities generally cannot receive duplicate support. Planning, acquisition, design and construction are eligible phases; construction-only requires readiness.
key_findings.implication: The proposal needs a qualifying WSC and a distinct eligible improvement package, not a speculative land-development request.

key_findings.finding: A research partnership may fit the grant if it directly supports an eligible water project.
key_findings.details: The Q&A allows potential WSC collaboration with universities/research organizations for eligible planning, while saying standalone research is not specifically identified as eligible. It also recognizes potentially eligible interconnections to correct a drinking-water deficiency and achieve compliance.
key_findings.implication: Tie aquifer or infrastructure analysis to a clear supply/service decision and sponsoring utility.

source.title: Hydrogeologic Conceptual Model of Santa Elena Limestone and Southern Brewster County
source.author: Steve Finch, Principal Hydrogeologist
source.document_type: 27-slide conceptual-model presentation; not a verified final technical report
source.date_note: Filename uses 18Feb2026. Title slide identifies the Brewster County GCD meeting as February 19, 2026. Use February 2026 or the stated meeting date when describing it.
source.page_numbering: PDF page numbers and printed slide numbers match, 1–27.

Aquifer model.executive_assessment: This materially advances the previously identified aquifer-research gap: an actual professional conceptual model is public. It distinguishes aquifer zones, geological structure, recharge pathways, water levels and water quality. It does not establish how much additional water can be pumped sustainably, prove a drought-reliable regional supply, or demonstrate that a proposed well site will succeed. The final slide expressly acknowledges significant remaining characterization gaps.

findings.finding: The investigation has progressed beyond the idea stage.
findings.document_evidence: The presentation identifies an investigation area, data gathering, development of a geological/groundwater conceptual model and a report task. Structure contours use existing geological sections, faults and intrusions. The summary identifies three regional aquifer zones.
findings.interpretation: Our next research should build on this model and seek its supporting datasets or later report rather than commission the same introductory characterization again.
findings.limitation: The slides alone do not establish contract funding, completion of the final report or a validated numerical groundwater model.

findings.finding: Southern Brewster should not be analyzed as one uniform groundwater reservoir.
findings.document_evidence: The conceptual model divides the region into Solitario, Terlingua Ranch and Glen Rose zones based on regional structure. It identifies multiple water-bearing units in the first two zones.
findings.visual_observation: The zone maps place the Terlingua/Study Butte vicinity in the southwestern Solitario area; Terlingua Ranch is a separate central zone and Glen Rose lies to the northeast. Boundaries are conceptual regional lines, not parcel-scale proof of hydraulic barriers.
findings.interpretation: Well comparisons and drilling screening should match geological unit and structural setting, not just distance to the nearest productive well.

findings.finding: Terlingua Ranch is described as particularly complex and locally compartmentalized.
findings.document_evidence: Primary water-bearing rocks are Boquillas/igneous; Santa Elena occurs at varying depths with localized or compartmentalized systems. Well yields are characterized qualitatively as low to moderate; flow directions vary. Recharge is interpreted around mountain perimeters through fractured rock.
findings.interpretation: A good nearby well may tap a different compartment or depth. Simply making a hole deeper or wider is not a demonstrated route to reliable production.
findings.limitation: The two example yields are reported well values, not demonstrated sustainable yields for the zone. Head differences alone do not prove connectivity or isolation without well construction, dates and pumping context.

findings.finding: The Solitario zone offers a plausible regional-flow hypothesis, but high and low yields both occur.
findings.document_evidence: The presentation identifies Terlingua Creek alluvium, Boquillas Formation and Santa Elena Limestone. It describes Santa Elena as apparently a regional flow system, with high structural complexity, southeastward flow and a wide qualitative yield range. Recharge is interpreted around Solitario and along Terlingua Creek.
findings.interpretation: This supports prioritizing a professional assessment of existing deep utility sources and their interactions. It does not show that every local well shares one well-connected reservoir.
findings.limitation: No quantified connection coefficient, multiwell interference test or additional allowable pumping volume appears in the presentation. Slide24 contains an unidentified example labeled TDLR xxxxxx with 25 gpm; do not add it as an identified atlas well.

findings.finding: The northeastern Glen Rose zone is characterized more favorably in broad geological terms.
findings.document_evidence: It is described as predominantly Glen Rose groundwater beneath exposed Santa Elena, moderately complex, with potential for moderate/high well yields. Recharge is interpreted as more widespread infiltration of rainfall/runoff; flow is northwest to southeast, with discharge toward the Rio Grande.
findings.interpretation: It is a comparison source area worth retaining in regional research, not a proven water import scheme.
findings.limitation: No mapped parcel-level probability, spare capacity, sustained production figure or conveyance cost is provided. A favorable source characterization does not establish economical access to Terlingua.

findings.finding: Recharge pathways are identified, but recharge quantities are not.
findings.document_evidence: The three zones have different inferred routes by which rainfall and runoff enter groundwater. Slide15 combines these interpretations with precipitation shading and watershed boundaries.
findings.interpretation: These pathways can guide monitoring and source-protection work. They do not yet tell us how many gallons/day can be withdrawn through a drought.
findings.limitation: The precipitation map is not a recharge-volume map. The presentation contains no recharge rate in acre-feet/year, full groundwater budget or calibrated drought response.

findings.finding: Treatment requirements should vary by source zone and well.

reported_TDS_ranges_mg_per_L.Terlingua_Ranch: 500–2,500; the slide itself includes a question mark

findings.interpretation: The broad ranges reinforce the need to price water quality and treatment alongside drilling yield.
findings.limitation: These are conceptual source-water summaries, not current lab results for a selected well. TDS alone does not establish drinking-water safety.

findings.finding: The plotted water levels cover different aquifers and cannot be treated as a single trend for deep Santa Elena supply.

visually_checked_hydrographs.observation: Sparse measurements show a substantially higher early point than many later points; no cause attribution established.
Terlingua Ranch measurements vary, including a conspicuous low point; operating state is not shown.
Panther Junction vicinity has a much denser, variable time series; this is not the deep Study Butte utility aquifer.
Local plotted elevations cluster in a relatively narrow band compared with the other plots; this shallow record does not establish stability of the deep Santa Elena aquifer.

findings.interpretation: Use these well IDs to retrieve original measurements, construction records and measurement qualifications before fitting trends or evaluating source reliability.
findings.limitation: No stable-yield or pumping-capacity conclusion can be calculated from the plotted points alone.

what_it_resolves: Confirms professional aquifer-conceptualization work is publicly available as of February 2026.
Provides a defensible regional framework for splitting well-data analysis by geological zone and unit.
Provides concrete recharge hypotheses, mapped structures and example wells for targeted follow-up.
what_remains_unresolved: Quantified sustainable yield and drought-reliable additional regional supply.
Pumping interactions between existing utility wells, new wells and other groundwater users.
Current pumping quantities, aquifer properties, quantitative recharge and a validated water budget.
Parcel-scale drilling success probabilities, treatment requirements and project economics.
Status, deliverables, funding and publication of any final report beyond this presentation.
Aquifer model.recommended_project_change: Replace the blanket question 'Has anyone studied this aquifer?' with 'What data and decisions can the February 2026 conceptual model already support, and what remaining measurements are required to evaluate a specific utility expansion?' First look for the final report, source tables, map layers and follow-up GCD materials before proposing a new study.

visual_review.method: Local source rendered using bundled Poppler at 110 dpi; maps, cross sections, example logs, head table and hydrographs inspected. Full text reviewed. No precise numerical series digitized from plots.

Water use.reported_source: Metered groundwater self supplied, Igneous Aquifer; Brackish/Saline Y; 0% treated prior to intake. Well name blank.
limits: Reported historical annual intake and retail consumption are not rated capacity, current availability, surplus supply or sustainable aquifer yield.
Raw intake minus metered retail is not a leakage estimate. Treatment reject/process use and other accounting components require water-loss audit reconciliation.
Reported full-time residential population excludes any unreported seasonal/tourist interpretation; commercial accounts are not a direct visitor count.
CSV report layout omits some visual summary fields; PDF is authoritative for the connection/use table.
2024 uses 366 days and 2025 uses 365 days for computed daily averages.
Water use.visual_validation: Both one-page PDFs rendered and visually checked against extracted values.

Utility website findings:
STUDY BUTTE WATER SUPPLY CORPORATION — PUBLIC RECORDS REVIEW
Retrieved October 23, 2026. No outreach or records requests sent.

ARCHIVE
33 sources archived: all 14 pages in the current official sitemap, all 17 PDF documents linked from those pages, and two alternate historical CCR PDFs found through search. This includes every currently linked annual water-quality report for 2014–2025. Original HTML/PDF files, readable extraction where possible, source URLs, date notes, hashes, and source-specific limitations are in inventory.json. The sitemap is retained too. coverage.json describes the search boundary and missing records. A current-site capture is not an exhaustive archive of everything ever released.

WHAT PUBLIC RECORDS ALREADY ANSWER
1. Infrastructure reliability is an acknowledged bottleneck. The utility's project page describes undersized/leaking mains, outdated control equipment and two 35,000-gallon tanks needing rehabilitation. Its environmental document identifies TWDB project 62844 with total financing of $1.48 million for 7,550 feet of replacement mains along highways 118/170, SCADA and tank work. This is rehabilitation; the clearance excludes the Ron Read Road alternate and says no pipeline extensions for looping. Its map is credited to engineering firm Jacob Martin. It does not establish construction completion or additional source capacity.
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/copy-of-about
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/_files/ugd/313504_c08d56c07c694d8eb60b3e4e646bb474.pdf

2. A recent interruption has already been resolved according to the live homepage. It rescinds the October 7 boil-water notice effective October 19, 2026. Search-engine cached text still displays the earlier notice and attributes it to a mainline leak/pressure loss. Use the live rescission for current status, not stale search text.
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/

3. They already disclose operational constraints affecting growth: conditional acceptance of new customers, potential engineering/upgrades and financing needs, remote procurement, small staffing, and repairs taking precedence over extensions. The office bulk-fill point is described as temporary with an eventual upgrade, but no public schedule or committed upgrade budget was found on that page.
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/faq

4. Water availability and water service are separate questions. The homepage publishes June 2026 static depths of 848 feet for well 1 and 855 feet for well 2, compared with isolated older readings of 850 feet. These snapshots are not sustained-yield tests or proof that extra customers can be served. No current spare capacity, daily treatment throughput, or pump-test logs were published in the inspected site.
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/

5. The latest water-quality report identifies two groundwater sources at the office and gives 2025 treated-water results. It reports lead's 90th percentile at 1.82 ppb with zero sampling sites above the action level and no additional required health-effects violation notices. Earlier reports disclose both actual water-quality exceedances and monitoring/notification failures, which must remain distinct. The 2024 report includes a service-line summary of 295 total, all non-lead; the last-page table was visually checked because text extraction incorrectly joins footnote 2 and the zero count into '20'. Annual reports do not establish current aquifer yield.
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/forms-and-reports
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/_files/ugd/313504_1a36d4d8f7d24aa292b41cb27c3172f3.pdf
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/_files/ugd/313504_00a19473374a49cdbe05810f1f6b49e8.pdf

6. Existing bulk-water terms do not authorize a delivery business: purchaser present, personal use only, no delivery to others, 3,000 gallons per address per month and restricted hours/availability. The utility classifies hauled water as non-potable because customer containers can introduce contamination. The displayed price literally says '$0.06 cents/gallon'; that unit wording is ambiguous and was preserved rather than silently corrected.
   https://www.studybuttewater.com/

SOURCE CAVEATS THAT MATTER BEFORE OUTREACH
- The homepage link labeled August 24, 2026 actually opens a May 14, 2026 agenda, posted May 11. It contains SRF/RO project updates, waterline mapping, the 2025 audit and long-term planning as agenda topics. It is not minutes and does not tell us what was decided.
- The About page and May agenda have different at-large director names. Neither should be assumed to be a definitive October roster without a more current source.
- The linked 29-page tariff scan says prepared July 1994, revisions February 2007, with an October 2002 resolution. It is not a confirmed current consolidated tariff. The current rate webpage and individualized extension quote process should not be replaced by old tariff assumptions.
- The environmental document's PDF metadata is June 18, 2026, but no issue date is visible on the reviewed letter pages. Its $1.48 million total must be reconciled with earlier/later TWDB commitments, not simply added to the December 2025 $1.18 million award.

STILL NOT FOUND ONLINE IN THIS UTILITY-SITE SEARCH
Board minutes/archive; the actual 2025 financial audit; current engineering capacity/hydraulic study; detailed current distribution GIS; sustained-yield logs; complete operating production/pressure/loss series; latest consolidated bylaws/tariff amendments. Some items are explicitly available at the office or on request. These are identified gaps, not conclusions that records do not exist.

RESEARCH IMPLICATION
A useful project can begin by assembling and extending already identified rehabilitation and operations work. Public material does not yet support promising an expansion volume or assuming a new regional system is necessary. The immediate desk-research task is to reconcile existing funded project scopes, available operating data and service boundaries before proposing additional work.
Source classification caveat: The2024/2025 water-use surveys label raw groundwater Igneous Aquifer. Preserve this reported field; do not automatically map it to Santa Elena limestone without confirming actual utility well logs. The geological presentation distinguishes multiple formations and regional zones.
